ADVARSEL: 5 ting at se på
peterfausboll@ubserv:~/code/pricejob/backend$ sudo systemctl status postgresql
[sudo] password for peterfausboll:
● postgresql.service - PostgreSQL RDBMS
Loaded: loaded (/lib/systemd/system/postgresql.service; enabled; vendor preset: enabled)
Active: active (exited) since Tue 2026-10-13 16:51:25 CEST; 1 day 1h ago
Process: 2237 ExecStart=/bin/true (code=exited, status=0/SUCCESS)
Main PID: 2237 (code=exited, status=0/SUCCESS)
CPU: 1ms

Oct 13 16:51:25 ubserv systemd[1]: Starting PostgreSQL RDBMS...
Oct 13 16:51:25 ubserv systemd[1]: Finished PostgreSQL RDBMS.

Den der ser faktisk sund ud — PostgreSQL kører.

Men der er en klassisk fælde gemt i outputtet, og den er værd at kende:

Active: active (exited) betyder ikke at databasen kører.

Den service du ser på, er kun en wrapper. På Debian/Ubuntu er postgresql.service en "oneshot"-enhed, hvis eneste job er at kalde /bin/true — altså gøre ingenting og afslutte med status 0. Det kan du se direkte:

  • Process: 2237 ExecStart=/bin/true — hovedprocessen er bogstaveligt talt true.
  • Main PID: 2237 (code=exited, status=0/SUCCESS) — hovedprocessen er allerede afsluttet.
  • CPU: 1ms — der er ikke noget, der har kørt i et døgn.

Den egentlige database ligger i en separat, versioneret enhed — typisk postgresql@16-main.service (eller 15, 14 …). Det er den, du skal se på, hvis du vil vide, om postgres faktisk lytter på port 5432.

De 5 ting at tjekke

  1. Find den rigtige enhed:

    bash
    systemctl list-units 'postgresql*' --all

    Leder du efter en specifik version/cluster:

    bash
    systemctl status postgresql@16-main

  2. Bekræft at der faktisk lyttes på porten:

    bash
    ss -tlnp | grep 5432

    Ingen output = ingen database, uanset hvad postgresql.service påstår.

  3. Tjek cluster-status:

    bash
    pg_lsclusters

    Denne er den hurtigste sandhed: viser version, cluster, port, status og om det er startet. Alt andet er indirekte.

  4. Se om det er enabled ved reboot — enabled på wrapper'en siger intet om clusteret:

    bash
    systemctl is-enabled postgresql@16-main

  5. Prøv en rigtig forbindelse frem for at gætte:

    bash
    sudo -u postgres psql -c 'select version();'

    eller mod dit app-cluster:

    bash
    psql -h localhost -p 5432 -U <din_bruger> -d <din_db> -c '\conninfo'

Hvorfor det er relevant for dit projekt

Du står i pricejob/backend. Hvis backend fejler med "connection refused" mod 5432, mens systemctl status postgresql ser grøn ud, er det præcis denne forvirring, der sender folk på vildspor i en time. Tjek pg_lsclusters og ss -tlnp, ikke wrapper-servicen.

Sig til hvis du vil have mig til at kigge på en konkret fejl fra pricejob/backend — så send log-udskriften eller fejlbeskeden, og vi finder den sammen.

peterfausboll@ubserv:~/code/pricejob/backend$ systemctl list-units 'postgresql*' --all
UNIT LOAD ACTIVE SUB DESCRIPTION
postgresql.service loaded active exited PostgreSQL RDBMS
postgresql@14-main.service loaded active running PostgreSQL Cluster 14-main

LOAD = Reflects whether the unit definition was properly loaded.
ACTIVE = The high-level unit activation state, i.e. generalization of SUB.
SUB = The low-level unit activation state, values depend on unit type.
2 loaded units listed.
To show all installed unit files use 'systemctl list-unit-files'.

Der er svaret, og det bekræfter fælden: databasen kører — men ikke i den service, du kiggede på først.

postgresql@14-main.service står som active running. Det er den egentlige database, og den har været oppe siden i går. postgresql.service er som sagt bare wrapper'en, der har gjort sit og er afsluttet.

Så:

  • Version/cluster: 14-main — det er PostgreSQL 14, cluster-navnet main.
  • Status: kørende.
  • Port: ikke bevist endnu. main-clusteret lytter normalt på 5432, men det er en antagelse, ikke et faktum fra outputtet.

To kommandoer lukker de sidste huller:

bash
pg_lsclusters

Den giver dig version, cluster, port, status og datadirs på én linje — den autoritative oversigt.

bash
ss -tlnp | grep 5432

Bekræfter at der faktisk lyttes på porten, og hvilken proces der gør det.

Og hvis du vil se, at den svarer:

bash
sudo -u postgres psql -c 'select version();'

En ting værd at bemærke

14 er en ældre udgave. Hvis pricejob/backend er et nyt projekt, kan det være værd at tjekke, hvilken version dine Postgres-drivere og pg-afhængigheder forventer — og om der er en plan for at opgradere clusteret. Det er ikke et problem i sig selv; 14 virker fint. Men det er den slags, der bider senere, når to udviklere har hver sin version lokalt.

Sig til hvis du vil have hjælp til at læse outputtet fra pg_lsclusters eller en konkret forbindelsesfejl fra backend.

pasted-text.txt

TXT

Ok. Jeg har opbygget en hjemmeside, som ligger på Netsite, en database og backend som ligger på min egen ubuntu server og en frontend, som er hjemmesiden i js og html. Den viser de seneste elpriser. Databasen er defineret som nedenfor.
Nu vil jeg gerne udvide frontend med en HTML side mere med meteorologiske data. Dvs. at frontend, database og backend skal udvides. Jeg ønsker at bruge samme struktur og så meget af koden, som muligt igen.

Her er en plan og kode, der genbruger så meget af det eksisterende som muligt — samme mønstre, samme tabelnavne, samme run/state-logik.

Først det vigtigste princip: meteorologi er bare endnu et "job" i den struktur, du allerede har. sync_runs, sync_state og pushed_state er generiske — de kender ikke til elpriser. Du skal ikke bygge et parallelt system; du skal tilføje job = 'weather_forecast' og en ny datatabel. Så arver du automatisk run-historik, watermarks, fejlsporing og push-dedup.

Database

To ændringer: én ny tabel, og én justering af prices-primary key-mønsteret gentaget for vejr.

sql
-- Vejrdatatable. Samme form som prices: én række pr. (sted, tidspunkt).CREATE TABLE public.weather (    location      text NOT NULL,              -- fx 'Copenhagen' eller DMI-stationsnr    ts_dk         timestamp with time zone NOT NULL,    temperature_c numeric(5,2),    wind_ms       numeric(5,2),    wind_dir_deg  smallint,    humidity_pct  smallint,    precip_mm     numeric(6,2),    cloud_pct     smallint,    source        text NOT NULL DEFAULT 'dmi',    fetched_at    timestamp with time zone DEFAULT now() NOT NULL);
ALTER TABLE public.weather OWNER TO postgres;
ALTER TABLE ONLY public.weather    ADD CONSTRAINT weather_pkey PRIMARY KEY (location, ts_dk);
-- Idempotent upsert-mål: samme rolle som prices_pkey.CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS weather_ts_dk_idx ON public.weather (ts_dk);

Ingen ændringer i sync_runs, sync_state eller push_runs. sync_runs har allerede job text DEFAULT 'dayahead_prices', http_status, error_body jsonb osv. — præcis hvad en DMI-hentning har brug for (DMI's API returnerer JSON-fejl med HTTP-status, ligesom ENTSO-E/Energinet).

Hvis du kører flere lokationer, bør du overveje en locations-tabel frem for frie tekststrenge, men start med text — det matcher area text i prices, og du kan normalisere senere.

Backend — genbrug, ikke kopiér

Den vigtigste strukturelle pointe: din sync-logik er (forhåbentlig) allerede opdelt i hent → parse → upsert → registrér run. Vejr skal ind i de samme fire led, ikke ind i en kopi af dem.

text
backend/  jobs/    dayahead_prices.py     # eksisterende    weather_forecast.py    # NY — samme form  sync/    runner.py              # fælles: åbner sync_run, kalder job, lukker run    db.py                  # fælles upsert-helpers  api/    prices.py              # eksisterende    weather.py             # NY — samme form

Det centrale er at trække run-håndteringen ud, så den er job-agnostisk:

python
# sync/runner.py — fælles for alle jobsfrom contextlib import contextmanager
@contextmanagerdef run_tracking(conn, job_name: str, window_from=None, window_to=None):    """Åbner en sync_run, yielder et mutable stats-objekt, lukker run'en korrekt."""    with conn.cursor() as cur:        cur.execute("""            INSERT INTO sync_runs (status, job, window_from, window_to)            VALUES ('running', %s, %s, %s)            RETURNING run_id        """, (job_name, window_from, window_to))        run_id = cur.fetchone()[0]    conn.commit()
    stats = {"rows_fetched": 0, "rows_written": 0, "http_status": None,             "http_message": None, "error_url": None, "attempts": 0,             "elapsed_ms": None, "error_body": None, "error": None}    try:        yield stats        status = "success"    except Exception as exc:        status = "failed"        stats["error"] = str(exc)        raise    finally:        with conn.cursor() as cur:            cur.execute("""                UPDATE sync_runs                   SET finished_at = now(), status = %s,                       rows_fetched = %s, rows_written = %s,                       http_status = %s, http_message = %s, error_url = %s,                       attempts = %s, elapsed_ms = %s, error_body = %s,                       error = %s                 WHERE run_id = %s            """, (status, stats["rows_fetched"], stats["rows_written"],                  stats["http_status"], stats["http_message"], stats["error_url"],                  stats["attempts"], stats["elapsed_ms"],                  json.dumps(stats["error_body"]) if stats["error_body"] else None,                  stats["error"], run_id))        conn.commit()

Vejr-jobbet bliver så tynd, fordi al infrastrukturen er delt:

python
# jobs/weather_forecast.pydef sync_weather(conn, location: str, window_from, window_to):    with run_tracking(conn, "weather_forecast", window_from, window_to) as stats:        payload, http = fetch_dmi_forecast(location)   # din HTTP-hentning        stats["http_status"] = http.status        stats["rows_fetched"] = http.rows
        rows = parse_dmi(payload)                      # ren funktion, nem at teste
        with conn.cursor() as cur:            cur.executemany("""                INSERT INTO weather (location, ts_dk, temperature_c, wind_ms,                                     wind_dir_deg, humidity_pct, precip_mm,                                     cloud_pct, source)                VALUES (%s, %s, %s, %s, %s, %s, %s, %s, 'dmi')                ON CONFLICT (location, ts_dk) DO UPDATE SET                    temperature_c = EXCLUDED.temperature_c,                    wind_ms       = EXCLUDED.wind_ms,                    wind_dir_deg  = EXCLUDED.wind_dir_deg,                    humidity_pct  = EXCLUDED.humidity_pct,                    precip_mm     = EXCLUDED.precip_mm,                    cloud_pct     = EXCLUDED.cloud_pct,                    fetched_at    = now()            """, rows)            stats["rows_written"] = len(rows)
        update_sync_state(conn, "weather_forecast", window_to, stats["rows_written"])

ON CONFLICT … DO UPDATE er det samme idempotente mønster, du bruger på prices, og det er grunden til at vejr kan køre så ofte du vil uden dubletter.

API-endpointet følger prices.py 1:1 — samme query-form, samme JSON-shape:

python
# api/weather.py@router.get("/api/weather")def get_weather(location: str = "Copenhagen", hours: int = 48):    rows = db.fetch_all("""        SELECT location, ts_dk, temperature_c, wind_ms, wind_dir_deg,               humidity_pct, precip_mm, cloud_pct          FROM weather         WHERE location = %s AND ts_dk >= now() - interval '1 hour'         ORDER BY ts_dk         LIMIT %s    """, (location, hours))    return {"location": location, "count": len(rows), "rows": [dict(r) for r in rows]}

Frontend — ny side, samme mønster

Genbrug fetch-rendering-flowet. Hvis din prisside ligner nedenstående, er vejrsiden en næsten mekanisk udgave:

html
<!-- weather.html — samme skal, samme script-load-mønster --><!DOCTYPE html><html lang="da"><head>  <meta charset="utf-8">  <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">  <title>Vejr — priser &amp; prognose</title>  <link rel="stylesheet" href="/css/style.css"></head><body>  <nav>    <a href="/index.html">Elpriser</a>    <a href="/weather.html" class="active">Vejr</a>  </nav>
  <main id="app">    <h1>Meteorologiske data</h1>    <p class="meta" id="meta">Indlæser…</p>    <table id="tbl">      <thead>        <tr><th>Tid</th><th>Temp (°C)</th><th>Vind (m/s)</th>            <th>Retning</th><th>Fugt (%)</th><th>Nedbør (mm)</th></tr>      </thead>      <tbody></tbody>    </table>  </main>
  <script src="/js/weather.js"></script></body></html>
javascript
// js/weather.js — spejler din prices.jsconst API = '/api/weather';
async function load() {  const meta = document.getElementById('meta');  const tbody = document.querySelector('#tbl tbody');  try {    const res = await fetch(`${API}?location=Copenhagen&hours=48`);    if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`HTTP ${res.status}`);    const data = await res.json();
    tbody.innerHTML = '';    for (const r of data.rows) {      const tr = document.createElement('tr');      tr.innerHTML = `        <td>${new Date(r.ts_dk).toLocaleString('da-DK')}</td>        <td>${fmt(r.temperature_c, 1)}</td>        <td>${fmt(r.wind_ms, 1)}</td>        <td>${r.wind_dir_deg ?? '–'}</td>        <td>${r.humidity_pct ?? '–'}</td>        <td>${fmt(r.precip_mm, 1)}</td>`;      tbody.appendChild(tr);    }    meta.textContent = `${data.rows.length} rækker · ${data.location}`;  } catch (err) {    meta.textContent = `Fejl: ${err.message}`;  }}
const fmt = (v, d) => (v == null ? '–' : Number(v).toFixed(d));load();

De 5 ting, der er værd at beslutte nu

  1. Datakilde. DMI's åbne data (opendata.dmi.dk) er det nærmeste, der matcher Energinet-mønsteret: gratis, JSON, versionsløst, ingen nøgle. Alternativt MET Norway (yr). Vælg én og hold dig til den — ikke to kilder i weather-tabellen uden source-kolonnen i brug.

  2. Granularitet og horisont. DMI's prognoser er typisk timebaserede, 48–120 timer frem. Beslut om ts_dk er time-start (så PK holder) og om du vil gemme hele horisonten hver gang eller kun fremtiden.

  3. Lokationer. "Copenhagen" som streng er fint nu, men hvis du vil vise vejr for de samme zoner, du har i prices.area, så brug identiske strenge — ellers får du et join-problem senere.

  4. Retention. Prognoser overskrives (samme ts_dk får ny værdi). Men historiske prognoser er værdifulde, hvis du vil lave "hvad forudsagde vi i går"-analyser. Overvej weather_forecast_history hvis det er interessant — eller lad det være, indtil du har brug for det.

  5. Push-laget. Hvis Netsite-frontenden er statisk og får data via pushed_state-mekanismen, skal vejr med i samme push-flow. Spørgsmålet er, om vejr skal pushes som separat fil/endpoint, eller om det skal flettes ind i det eksisterende payload. Separat er klart at foretrække — så fejler det ene ikke det andet.

Vil du have mig til at skrive den konkrete fetch_dmi_forecast + parse_dmi mod DMI's faktiske API-shape? Så skal jeg have enten et eksempel på deres JSON-respons, eller jeg kan slå den aktuelle endpoint-struktur op. Sig også gerne, hvordan push_runs/Netsite-delen hænger sammen — så tilpasser jeg trin 5 til din faktiske pipeline i stedet for at gætte.

Jeg kommer til at bruge flere kilder. Bl.a DMI, DWD, Smard. Dvs også flere lokationer

Det ændrer datamodellen mere, end det måske ser ud ved første øjekast. Med flere kilder og flere lokationer holder weather-tabellen i den form, jeg skitserede, ikke — den ville blande "hvilket sted" og "hvilken kilde" sammen i én streng, og så kan du ikke svare på, hvem der sagde hvad.

Løsningen er en kilde- og lokationsdimension plus en normaliseret observationstabel. Det er samme greb, du allerede bruger i prices: nøglen er (dimension, tid), ikke (navn, tid).

Datamodel

sql
-- Kilder: dmi, dwd, smard ...CREATE TABLE public.weather_sources (    source_id   text PRIMARY KEY,          -- 'dmi', 'dwd', 'smard'    display_name text NOT NULL,    kind        text NOT NULL,             -- 'forecast' | 'observation' | 'market'    base_url    text,    enabled     boolean NOT NULL DEFAULT true);
-- Lokationer: uafhængige af kilde, så samme sted kan hentes fra flere kilder.CREATE TABLE public.weather_locations (    location_id  text PRIMARY KEY,         -- 'copenhagen', 'berlin', 'dk1' ...    display_name text NOT NULL,    country      char(2) NOT NULL,         -- ISO-3166 alpha-2    lat          numeric(8,5),    lon          numeric(8,5),    tz           text NOT NULL DEFAULT 'Europe/Copenhagen');
-- Hvilken kilde kan levere hvilken lokation? (mange-til-mange)CREATE TABLE public.weather_source_locations (    source_id   text NOT NULL REFERENCES public.weather_sources(source_id),    location_id text NOT NULL REFERENCES public.weather_locations(location_id),    -- kildens eget id for stedet, fx DMI station-nr eller DWD stations_id    external_id text,    PRIMARY KEY (source_id, location_id));

Så selve datatabellen. Læg mærke til run_type-skellet — det er den vigtigste beslutning her:

sql
CREATE TABLE public.weather (    source_id     text NOT NULL REFERENCES public.weather_sources(source_id),    location_id   text NOT NULL REFERENCES public.weather_locations(location_id),    ts_dk         timestamp with time zone NOT NULL,   -- det tidspunkt data gælder    run_type      text NOT NULL DEFAULT 'forecast',    -- 'forecast' | 'observation'    -- prognosens udstedelsestid: NULL for observationer, sat for prognoser    issued_at     timestamp with time zone,    temperature_c numeric(5,2),    wind_ms       numeric(5,2),    wind_dir_deg  smallint,    humidity_pct  smallint,    precip_mm     numeric(6,2),    cloud_pct     smallint,    pressure_hpa  numeric(6,1),    fetched_at    timestamp with time zone DEFAULT now() NOT NULL,    CONSTRAINT weather_pkey        PRIMARY KEY (source_id, location_id, run_type, ts_dk, issued_at));
CREATE INDEX weather_lookup_idx    ON public.weather (location_id, ts_dk)    WHERE run_type = 'forecast';

Hvorfor issued_at i PK'en? Fordi DMI, DWD og SMARD udsteder prognoser på forskellige tidspunkter, og en prognose for "i morgen kl. 14" kan udstedes i dag, i går og i sidste uge. Uden issued_at overskriver du historikken, og så kan du ikke længere måle, om DMI blev bedre end DWD. Med den i PK'en får du prognose-verifikation gratis: join samme ts_dk på tværs af issued_at og sammenlign mod run_type = 'observation'.

Hvis du ikke vil have den analyse, kan du lade issued_at være almindelig kolonne og PK være (source_id, location_id, run_type, ts_dk) — men så mister du evnen, og det er sværere at tilføje senere end at have den fra start.

Konsekvenser for backend

Med flere kilder bliver "én job-funktion pr. kilde" for meget kodeduplikering. Brug et adapter-mønster: hver kilde er en tynd klasse, der oversætter til en fælles form, og resten af pipelinen er delt.

python
# jobs/weather/base.pyfrom dataclasses import dataclass
@dataclassclass WeatherRow:    location_id: str    ts_dk: object            # aware datetime    run_type: str    issued_at: object | None    temperature_c: float | None = None    wind_ms: float | None = None    wind_dir_deg: int | None = None    humidity_pct: int | None = None    precip_mm: float | None = None    cloud_pct: int | None = None    pressure_hpa: float | None = None
class SourceAdapter:    """Kontrakten alle kilder opfylder. Kun fetch() og parse() er kilde-specifikke."""    source_id: str
    def fetch(self, location_id: str, external_id: str) -> tuple[object, dict]:        """Returnér (rå payload, http-meta med status/url)."""        raise NotImplementedError
    def parse(self, payload, location_id: str) -> list[WeatherRow]:        """Oversæt rå payload til fælles WeatherRow-liste."""        raise NotImplementedError

Pipelinen er så fælles for alle kilder:

python
# jobs/weather/pipeline.pydef sync_source(conn, adapter, location_id, external_id):    with run_tracking(conn, f"weather_{adapter.source_id}") as stats:        payload, http = adapter.fetch(location_id, external_id)        stats["http_status"] = http.get("status")        stats["error_url"]  = http.get("url")
        rows = adapter.parse(payload, location_id)        stats["rows_fetched"] = len(rows)
        with conn.cursor() as cur:            cur.executemany("""                INSERT INTO weather (source_id, location_id, ts_dk, run_type,                                     issued_at, temperature_c, wind_ms, wind_dir_deg,                                     humidity_pct, precip_mm, cloud_pct, pressure_hpa)                VALUES (%s,%s,%s,%s,%s,%s,%s,%s,%s,%s,%s,%s)                ON CONFLICT (source_id, location_id, run_type, ts_dk, issued_at)                DO UPDATE SET                    temperature_c = EXCLUDED.temperature_c,                    wind_ms       = EXCLUDED.wind_ms,                    wind_dir_deg  = EXCLUDED.wind_dir_deg,                    humidity_pct  = EXCLUDED.humidity_pct,                    precip_mm     = EXCLUDED.precip_mm,                    cloud_pct     = EXCLUDED.cloud_pct,                    pressure_hpa  = EXCLUDED.pressure_hpa,                    fetched_at    = now()            """, [as_tuple(r, adapter.source_id) for r in rows])            stats["rows_written"] = len(rows)
        update_sync_state(conn, f"weather_{adapter.source_id}", None, stats["rows_written"])

Bemærk: hver kilde får sit eget job-navn i sync_runs og sync_state. Så fejler DWD, ser du job = 'weather_dwd' med status = 'failed', og DMI er upåvirket. Det er præcis den isolationsgevinst, din eksisterende run-tabel giver dig gratis.

De tre adaptere er så små:

python
class DmiAdapter(SourceAdapter):    source_id = "dmi"    def fetch(self, location_id, external_id):        # DMI opendata: [opendata.dmi.dk](https://opendata.dmi.dk/)        ...    def parse(self, payload, location_id):        # DMI leverer timebaseret prognose; map felter → WeatherRow        ...
class DwdAdapter(SourceAdapter):    source_id = "dwd"    # DWD har både observations- og MOSMIX-prognosedata.    ...
class SmardAdapter(SourceAdapter):    source_id = "smard"    # SMARD er et *marked*, ikke vejr — se note nedenfor.    ...

Tre ting, der kræver en beslutning fra dig

1. SMARD er ikke vejr. SMARD (Bundesnetzagentur) leverer elmarkedsdata — generation, forbrug, priser — for Tyskland. Det passer dårligt i weather-tabellen. To muligheder: enten får SMARD sin egen tabel (market_data) og sit eget job, eller du generaliserer weather-tabellen til en bred time_series-tabel med en metric-kolonne. Jeg hælder til det første — SMARD's felter (MW, €/MWh, fuel type) ligner ikke vejr, og en fælles tabel bliver en tabel med 20 nullable kolonner, hvor halvdelen altid er NULL.

Hvis SMARD derimod skal bruges som pris-kilde ved siden af Energinet, hører den hjemme i prices-familien, ikke i vejr.

2. Aggregering på tværs af kilder er en frontend-beslutning, ikke en database-beslutning. Gem alle kilder separat og råt. Lav først gennemsnit/median/afvigelser i API-laget eller i frontenden, hvor du kan vise "DMI siger 12°, DWD siger 14°". Joiner du kilderne i databasen, smider du information væk.

3. Kadence og retry pr. kilde. DMI opdaterer typisk 2× i døgnet, DWD's MOSMIX flere gange, SMARD hvert 15. minut. Så sync_state.last_run_at pr. job skal styre hvert sit skema — ikke ét fælles vejr-job. Det er endnu et argument for job = 'weather_<kilde>'.

Frontend

Med flere kilder bliver visningen interessant, og det er her, du får værdi af at have holdt kilderne adskilt. Et minimalt mønster: én række pr. tidspunkt, én kolonne pr. kilde.

javascript
// js/weather.js — sammenligningsvisningasync function load() {  const res = await fetch('/api/weather?location=copenhagen&hours=48');  const data = await res.json();   // { location, sources: { dmi: [...], dwd: [...] }, times: [...] }
  const tbody = document.querySelector('#tbl tbody');  tbody.innerHTML = '';  for (const t of data.times) {    const tr = document.createElement('tr');    tr.innerHTML = `<td>${new Date(t).toLocaleString('da-DK')}</td>` +      data.sourceIds.map(sid => {        const row = data.sources[sid]?.find(r => r.ts_dk === t);        return `<td>${row ? Number(row.temperature_c).toFixed(1) : '–'}</td>`;      }).join('');    tbody.appendChild(tr);  }}

API'et pivoterer altså kilden til kolonner. Det er en ren præsentationsbeslutning og kan ændres uden at røre databasen.

Hvad jeg mangler for at gå videre

Jeg kan ikke skrive de tre adaptere konkret uden at kende de faktiske API-shapes. To muligheder:

  • Send mig et eksempel på en JSON-respons fra hver kilde (eller bare DMI, så tager vi den først), og jeg skriver fetch + parse præcist mod den.
  • Eller sig til, og jeg slår de aktuelle endpoint-strukturer op for DMI opendata, DWD MOSMIX og SMARD, så vi rammer deres nuværende form frem for en jeg husker.

Og én ting mere, som ændrer designet: er SMARD tænkt som vejr-kilde eller som markedsdata? Det afgør, om vi skal have én tabel eller to, og jeg vil hellere spørge nu end at bygge om bagefter.

Databasen skal være generel til at kunne håndtere både prognoser og historiske data. Jeg vil også gerne kunne vise grafer, hvor min og max over seneste 10 bliver vist.

Kravet om at kunne vise min/max over de seneste 10 ændrer datamodellen ét afgørende sted: du må ikke længere overskrive prognoser. Det er den beslutning, resten følger af.

Princippet: prognoser er ikke fakta

En prognose udstedt i går for i morgen og en prognose udstedt i dag for i morgen er to forskellige observationer af verden — ikke én sandhed, der bliver opdateret. Behandler du dem som samme række (som ON CONFLICT ... DO UPDATE gør), er historikken væk, og så kan du ikke:

  • vise hvordan prognosen har flyttet sig de seneste 10 kørsler
  • vise min/max over de seneste 10 prognoser for samme tidspunkt
  • måle, om DMI eller DWD ramte rigtigst

Det er præcis det, issued_at i primary key'en fra sidste svar var forberedt til. Nu bliver det bærende.

Skellet mellem prognose og historik

Databasen skal kunne tre ting, og de er ikke det samme:

SlagsEksempelRække-identitetOverskrives?
PrognoseDMI siger 12° torsdag 14:00kilde, sted, issued_at, ts_dkNej — append
ObservationDMI målte 11,4° torsdag 14:00kilde, sted, ts_dkJa — korrigeret måling vinder
MarkedSMARD: 42 GW forbrugkilde, metrik, ts_dkJa

Det er den tredje og den første, der ligner hinanden farligt meget, hvis man kun kigger på kolonnenavne. Adskil dem eksplicit:

sql
CREATE TABLE public.weather (    source_id     text NOT NULL REFERENCES public.weather_sources(source_id),    location_id   text NOT NULL REFERENCES public.weather_locations(location_id),    ts_dk         timestamp with time zone NOT NULL,   -- gyldighedstidspunkt    kind          text NOT NULL,                       -- 'forecast' | 'observation'    issued_at     timestamp with time zone NOT NULL,   -- for observation: = ts_dk    -- datakvalitet    source_run_id text,          -- kildens egen run-id / modelversion, fx MOSMIX-run    quality       text,          -- 'ok' | 'estimated' | 'interpolated'    temperature_c numeric(5,2),    wind_ms       numeric(5,2),    wind_dir_deg  smallint,    humidity_pct  smallint,    precip_mm     numeric(6,2),    cloud_pct     smallint,    pressure_hpa  numeric(6,1),    fetched_at    timestamp with time zone DEFAULT now() NOT NULL,    CONSTRAINT weather_pkey        PRIMARY KEY (source_id, location_id, kind, ts_dk, issued_at));

issued_at NOT NULL er med vilje: for observationer sætter du den lig ts_dk, så PK'en virker ens for begge. Det holder queries simple, fordi du aldrig skal håndtere NULL i en nøgle.

Bemærk hvad der ikke sker: ingen ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE for prognoser. De indsættes append-only. En prognose, der er hentet to gange uden at have ændret sig, rammer PK'en og ignoreres (DO NOTHING) — det er gratis dedup. Har den ændret sig, får den ny issued_at, og begge versioner lever.

sql
INSERT INTO weather (source_id, location_id, kind, ts_dk, issued_at, source_run_id,                     temperature_c, wind_ms, wind_dir_deg, humidity_pct,                     precip_mm, cloud_pct, pressure_hpa)VALUES (...)ON CONFLICT (source_id, location_id, kind, ts_dk, issued_at) DO NOTHING;

Det er den ene ændring fra sidste svar, og den er ikke kosmetisk — det er forskellen på et system, der kan vise udvikling, og et system, der kun kan vise status nu.

Min/max over de seneste 10

Her er pointen: med append-only behøver du ingen separat historik-tabel, ingen trigger og ingen cron, der rydder op. De seneste 10 er bare de 10 nyeste issued_at-værdier for samme (source, location, ts_dk). Det er en window-funktion.

sql
-- Min/max temperatur for hvert (sted, tidspunkt) over de seneste 10 prognosekørslerWITH recent AS (    SELECT source_id, location_id, ts_dk, issued_at, temperature_c,           row_number() OVER (               PARTITION BY source_id, location_id, ts_dk               ORDER BY issued_at DESC           ) AS rn      FROM weather     WHERE kind = 'forecast'       AND location_id = %(location)s       AND ts_dk BETWEEN %(from)s AND %(to)s)SELECT source_id, ts_dk,       min(temperature_c)  AS t_min,       max(temperature_c)  AS t_max,       avg(temperature_c)  AS t_avg,       count(*)            AS n_runs  FROM recent WHERE rn <= 10 GROUP BY source_id, ts_dk ORDER BY ts_dk;

Det giver dig præcis den båndgraf, du beskriver: midterlinjen er seneste prognose, båndet er min/max over de sidste 10. Vil du have "seneste værdi" ved siden af, tilføjer du:

sql
       (array_agg(temperature_c ORDER BY issued_at DESC))[1] AS t_latest

i recent-CTE'en, eller henter den direkte med DISTINCT ON (source_id, location_id, ts_dk) ... ORDER BY issued_at DESC.

Hvis data bliver store nok til at det mærkes, er indekset her vigtigt:

sql
CREATE INDEX weather_forecast_window_idx    ON public.weather (location_id, ts_dk, issued_at DESC)    WHERE kind = 'forecast';

Det er det samme indeks-mønster, prices allerede bruger i (area, ts_dk) — bare med issued_at tilføjet.

Retention bliver nu en reel beslutning

Append-only vokser. Med 3 kilder × 20 lokationer × 48 timers horisont × 2 kørsler i døgnet er det ~5.800 rækker i døgnet — trivielt. Med 10 kilder × 200 lokationer × 120 timer × 4 kørsler er det 960.000 i døgnet, og så skal du tænke over det.

Tre fornuftige strategier, i den rækkefølge jeg ville vælge dem:

  1. Behold alt, og arkivér senere. Simplest, og du ved ikke endnu, hvad du får brug for. Materialiseret view til graferne hvis queries bliver tunge.
  2. Rul ældre prognoser sammen. Efter fx 30 dage beholder du kun én pr. ts_dk pr. kilde (den sidste), og smider resten. Du mister fortidens prognoseusikkerhed, men beholder et historisk datasæt.
  3. Partitionér på ts_dk med pg_partman eller manuel DROP af gamle partitioner. Værd at overveje, hvis du rammer punkt 2's skala.

Ikke en beslutning du skal tage nu — men den er nu, den bliver nødvendig at have en holdning til.

Frontend: båndgrafen

Til grafen skal du ikke hente 10× data til browseren og regne i JS. API'et pivoterer — det er samme princip som kilderne-til-kolonner fra sidste svar, bare med min/max i stedet:

json
{  "location": "copenhagen",  "from": "2026-10-14T00:00:00Z",  "to": "2026-10-18T00:00:00Z",  "sources": {    "dmi": {      "series": [        {          "ts_dk": "2026-10-14T12:00:00Z",          "latest": 12.4,          "min": 10.1,          "max": 14.8,          "n_runs": 10        }      ]    }  }}

Båndet tegnes så som to serier — min og max — med en fyldt flade mellem dem, og latest som linje ovenpå. Med Chart.js eller uPlot er det:

javascript
// Bånd = max-serien med fill ned til min-seriendatasets: [  { label: 'Min',  data: series.map(p => p.min),  borderWidth: 0, fill: false },  { label: 'Max',  data: series.map(p => p.max),  borderWidth: 0,    fill: { target: '-1', above: 'rgba(31,119,180,0.15)' } },  { label: 'Seneste', data: series.map(p => p.latest),    borderColor: '#1f77b4', borderWidth: 2, fill: false }]

Rækkefølgen i datasets er ikke tilfældig: fill: { target: '-1' } peger på det foregående datasæt, så max skal ligge lige efter min.

Og det gode ved at have holdt kilderne adskilt: hvis DMI's bånd er smalt og DWD's er bredt, så betyder det, at DWD har skiftet mening mere — den slags bliver synligt gratis.

Hvad jeg stadig mangler

Datamodellen kan jeg skrive færdig nu. De konkrete adaptere kan jeg ikke, før jeg kender API-shapes. Og ét spørgsmål ændrer stadig designet:

Skal SMARD ind i weather-tabellen eller have sin egen? SMARD er markedsdata (GW, €/MWh), ikke meteorologi. Hvis du vil kunne lave "pris vs. vindproduktion"-grafer — hvilket ville være en meget naturlig ting at ville — skal SMARD's data være querybare på ts_dk sammen med vejret, men ikke i samme tabel. Det taler for en søstertabel, fx:

sql
CREATE TABLE public.market (    source_id   text NOT NULL,    metric      text NOT NULL,        -- 'generation_wind', 'consumption', 'price_de'    ts_dk       timestamp with time zone NOT NULL,    issued_at   timestamp with time zone NOT NULL,    value       numeric NOT NULL,    unit        text NOT NULL,    fetched_at  timestamp with time zone DEFAULT now() NOT NULL,    PRIMARY KEY (source_id, metric, ts_dk, issued_at));

Spejler weather nøjagtigt — samme kind-skel (her bare i metric), samme append-only-mønster, samme min/max-query. Så kan du joine på ts_dk på tværs af de to tabeller uden at blande enheder.

Sig til med ét af disse, og vi kommer videre:

  • Et eksempel på en JSON-respons fra DMI, DWD eller SMARD — så skriver jeg adapteren præcist mod den.
  • Eller bekræft at jeg skal slå de aktuelle API-strukturer op, så bygger jeg på deres nuværende form.
  • Og: SMARD som vejr eller som marked? Hvis marked, skal weather og market så kunne joines i et fælles API-endpoint, eller holder vi dem adskilt i frontend også?

For lige at starte enkelt. Kan den SQL jeg gav dig illustreres på nem måde i et diagram?

Ja. Et ER-diagram er den nemmeste måde at se strukturen på.

mermaid

Læg mærke til, hvad diagrammet afslører, som SQL'en ikke gør tydeligt: der er ingen fremmednøgler nogen steder. De fem tabeller er to adskilte grupper, der kun hænger sammen via job-strenge — ikke via relationer.

mermaid

Det er ikke en fejl — det er et bevidst og ret fornuftigt design til et lille ETL-setup. Run-tabellerne er logfiler, ikke entiteter med relationer. De beskriver hvad der skete, ikke hvad der findes. Prissdata og push-state er "det der findes".

Det er præcis derfor vejr kan tilføjes uden at røre de fem tabeller: du tilføjer bare en ny tabel, der også kender sit eget job-navn. Intet skal migreres.

Hvordan de to grupper hænger sammen

mermaid

Den stiplede forbindelse mellem sync_state og datatabellerne er hele pointen med mønsteret: état'et bor i sync-laget, dataene i datalaget. Datatabellerne skal ikke vide, hvornår de sidst blev opdateret — det er ikke deres opgave.

Den korte version, hvis du kun skal bruge én figur

mermaid

Tre tabeller, tre roller: hvad vi ved (sync_state), hvad vi gjorde (sync_runs), hvad vi har (prices). Tilføj vejr ved at kopiere prices-formen og sætte et nyt job-navn.

Vil du have diagrammet som en fil, så du kan bruge det i din dokumentation på Netsite eller i repoet? Jeg kan lave det som en SVG eller PNG, der viser både den nuværende struktur og hvor vejr/marked kobler på — sig til hvad format der passer bedst.

Is this the best way to document a db?

Short answer: no — a diagram is a useful part of database documentation, not the documentation itself. An ER diagram answers one question ("what tables and columns exist, and how do they relate") and is silent on almost everything else you actually need six months from now.

The honest split is that documentation has to carry what the schema file can't say out loud.

What a diagram is genuinely good at

  • The shape at a glance: how many tables, which are big, which are peripheral.
  • Where the relationships are — and, as your diagram above showed, where they aren't. That "no foreign keys anywhere" revelation is exactly the kind of thing a diagram surfaces instantly and a CREATE TABLE dump hides.
  • Onboarding. A new person sees the structure in ten seconds.
  • Spotting the outlier. A table with 20 columns next to five with five columns is visible as a shape.

That's real value. Keep it.

What it cannot carry

An ER diagram is generated from the schema, so it only ever restates what's already in schema.sql. It can't tell you:

  • Why. Why is pushed_state.content_hash a text and not a bytea? Why does prices key on (area, ts_dk) and not a surrogate id? Diagrams have no room for rationale, and rationale is the thing you forget.
  • Semantics. What does sync_runs.status actually contain — 'running', 'success', 'failed'? Is sync_state.watermark_dk inclusive or exclusive? A diagram shows text status and tells you nothing.
  • Invariants. "A sync_run with status='success' must have finished_at IS NOT NULL." "Never update a row in weather where kind='forecast'." These are rules no diagram can express and no constraint in your schema enforces.
  • Conventions. How jobs are named, how idempotency is achieved, what the ON CONFLICT target is and why. This is the actual institutional knowledge.
  • Operational stuff. Backup, retention, which queries are hot, what index exists and why.

What "good" actually looks like

The pragmatic answer for a project your size — one developer, a handful of tables: the schema file plus a short prose file, with the diagram embedded in the prose file as one section.

db/  schema.sql          # the truth, machine-readable, version-controlled  README.md           # the human layer  er-diagram.svg      # one picture, referenced from README

The README should be short and answer the questions above, not repeat the schema. Something like:

  • One paragraph: what this database is for.
  • The diagram.
  • A table of the tables: name, purpose in one line, rough row growth.
  • The conventions section — this is the part worth the most and written the least: naming, the job-name pattern, the append-only rule for forecasts, the idempotency pattern.
  • The rules that aren't in the schema — the invariants.
  • How to create it and how to verify it (the pg_lsclusters / psql checks from earlier).

The one thing I'd push back on

Don't hand-write the diagram as a Mermaid block and let it rot. A diagram maintained by hand drifts from the schema the moment anyone runs a migration, and a stale diagram is worse than no diagram — it's confidently wrong.

Two ways to avoid that, in order of effort:

  1. Generate it from the live database with a tool like schemaspy, postgresql_autodoc, or pgModeler — they read the actual catalogs and produce an SVG you regenerate on demand.
  2. Or keep hand-drawn Mermaid, but treat it as part of the schema's review — same commit as any table change. Cheap, but discipline-dependent.

The Mermaid I gave you above is fine as a sketch — it's what you'd use to think out loud, which is what we did. It's not what I'd commit as the canonical source of truth for a database that will grow to include weather and market tables.

For your project specifically

Given that you're about to add weather and market data with multiple sources and an append-only forecast model, the documentation that will actually save you is the conventions one, not the picture. The rule "forecasts are append-only, observations are upsert, never confuse the two" is the thing that will get violated in six months — and no diagram can hold it. The issued_at-in-primary-key decision needs a paragraph next to it explaining why, or someone will "simplify" it away.

So: keep the diagram, but if you write only one thing, write the conventions file.

Want me to draft that README — covering the current tables plus the weather/market additions, with the conventions written down? I have the schema from your paste, so I could produce it now.

yes please draft README

I'll write it as a Markdown file you can drop straight into the repo. Let me build it properly.

Writing a file

The file's written. It's a working document for the repo, not a repeat of the schema — the conventions section is the part that carries the weight.

What's in it: the table inventory, the diagram (including the "no foreign keys" observation as a deliberate design note rather than a gap), and then the parts a schema dump can't express — job naming, idempotency, timestamp semantics, status vocabulary, and the conventions that hold by agreement rather than by constraint.

Two things worth flagging in what I drafted:

The forecast/observation rule (4.4) is written as a rule for tables you haven't added yet. prices doesn't need it, but weather does, and the rule is much harder to retrofit than to state now — so it's in there with the rationale attached, aimed at whoever reads this in six months and thinks issued_at in a primary key looks like over-engineering.

The retention section (7) is deliberately left as an open decision with three options rather than a recommendation. I don't know your growth profile yet, and picking for you would put a guess in a document whose whole purpose is to be trustworthy.

Two things you should adjust before committing it:

The verification section names pricejob as the database — I inferred that from your working directory, so correct it if the database is called something else. And the psql command assumes postgres as the user, which matches the schema's owner.

The Mermaid blocks render on GitHub and in most Markdown viewers, but not everywhere. If Netsite's renderer doesn't do Mermaid, the diagram section is the only part that degrades — everything else is plain Markdown.

db-README.md

Markdown · MD

how can i show md files in Ubuntu

A few options, from "just read it" to "renders it properly."

From the terminal

cat gives you the raw Markdown, syntax and all:

bash
cat db-README.md

For long files, a pager is better:

bash
less db-README.md

If your terminal supports it, glow renders the formatting in-place — this is the nicest terminal option:

bash
sudo apt install glowglow db-README.md

glow handles headings, bold, lists, tables, and code blocks. It does not render Mermaid diagrams — you'll see the raw ```mermaid block as text. Same for bat (sudo apt install bat, then bat db-README.md), which adds syntax highlighting but no Markdown layout.

As a rendered document in a browser

This is what you want if you care about the diagrams, since only a browser will draw the Mermaid blocks.

pandoc to HTML is the most direct route:

bash
sudo apt install pandocpandoc db-README.md -o db-README.html --standalonexdg-open db-README.html

It converts tables and headings correctly, but the Mermaid code blocks come out as plain text — pandoc doesn't execute them. To get the diagrams rendered, add the Mermaid JavaScript to the HTML. Easiest way:

bash
pandoc db-README.md -o db-README.html --standalone \  --metadata title="pricejob DB" \  -H <(echo '<script type="module">import mermaid from "[cdn.jsdelivr.net](https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/mermaid@10/dist/mermaid.esm.min.mjs)"; mermaid.initialize({startOnLoad:true});</script>')

That injects Mermaid into the page header, and the browser renders the diagrams when you open it. Needs a network connection to pull the script from the CDN.

In your editor

If you use VS Code, the built-in Markdown preview (Ctrl+Shift+V) renders everything including Mermaid, with no setup at all. That's probably the lowest-friction option for editing the file, and it's what I'd use while iterating on it. The same is true for most modern editors — Obsidian, Typora, and the JetBrains IDEs all handle it.

My suggestion

For your actual workflow — you're editing this in the repo and want to see the diagrams:

  • Editing: VS Code preview. Zero install, live-updating.
  • Sharing it with someone (or viewing it on the server where there's no GUI): the pandoc + Mermaid route to a self-contained HTML file. You could then drop that HTML next to the website on Netsite.

One thing to be aware of if you go the pandoc route: the output is a static HTML file, so the diagram only draws if the browser can reach that CDN script. If the machine viewing it is offline or the CDN is blocked, you're back to seeing raw Mermaid text. If that matters, say so and I can inline the Mermaid library into the HTML instead, making it fully self-contained.

can i install mermaid also on ubuntu

Short answer: yes, but it's not a package you install — it's a JavaScript library, so "installing" it means getting the .js file onto the machine.

This is the distinction worth getting clear, because it explains why the package search will come up empty. Mermaid isn't a program like git or glow. It's a library that runs inside a browser (or inside Node) and turns ```mermaid blocks into SVG at view time. There's no mermaid binary and no apt install mermaid. So "installing it on Ubuntu" really means one of three things, depending on where you want the rendering to happen.

Option 1 — Node, for pre-rendering to SVG (self-contained HTML)

This is the useful one for your case, because it removes the CDN dependency I flagged earlier. Install Node, then the Mermaid CLI:

bash
sudo apt install nodejs npmsudo npm install -g @mermaid-js/mermaid-cli

That gives you mmdc, which renders a .mmd file to an image:

bash
mmdc -i diagram.mmd -o diagram.svg

The CLI uses a headless Chromium under the hood — it'll pull one down on first run, or you can point it at a system Chromium. To render inline in a Markdown file rather than standalone:

bash
mmdc -i db-README.md -o db-README.html

That converts the whole file and bakes the diagrams in as SVG, so no script tags and no network needed when you open it. This is the route to a fully self-contained HTML, which is what you said you'd want for dropping next to the site on Netsite.

Option 2 — Just vendor the JS file into the HTML

If you don't want Node at all, download the single Mermaid bundle and reference it locally instead of the CDN:

bash
curl -L -o mermaid.min.js \  [cdn.jsdelivr.net](https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/mermaid@10/dist/mermaid.min.js)

Then in the pandoc header, point at the local file rather than the CDN URL:

bash
pandoc db-README.md -o db-README.html --standalone \  -H <(echo '<script src="mermaid.min.js"></script><script>mermaid.initialize({startOnLoad:true});</script>')

Keep mermaid.min.js next to the HTML. Fully offline, ~2 MB, no package manager involved. This is the lightest way to get the result if Node feels like a lot of machinery for one README.

Option 3 — Nothing, because VS Code already has it

If you're viewing in VS Code's Markdown preview, Mermaid is already built in. Nothing to install — the editor bundles it. Same for Obsidian and most modern Markdown tools. If your goal is just "see the diagrams while I edit," you're done; this was never an Ubuntu problem.

What I'd actually do

Given that you edit in the repo and might share the result on Netsite:

  • Vendoring the JS file (option 2) if you just want to view the README in a browser occasionally. One curl, one adjacent file, works offline.
  • Mermaid CLI (option 1) if you want a real build step — commit the .svg files to the repo and reference them as images. That gives you diagrams that render in any Markdown viewer, including the ones that don't understand Mermaid, which is the most portable outcome.

The trade-off is maintenance: with option 1, the SVGs are build artefacts you regenerate when the schema changes. With option 2, the diagram is always current but only renders in a Mermaid-aware viewer. For a document you'll mostly read yourself and occasionally show to someone, option 2 is less to keep track of. For something that goes on the public site, option 1 — pre-rendered SVGs — is the safer choice, since the viewer's capabilities stop mattering.

One thing to confirm before you commit to either: does Netsite serve static files with arbitrary extensions, or is it restricted to HTML/CSS/JS/image types? If it only serves specific types, the .svg route works but the vendored .js route may not. Worth a quick check against their docs before you build around it.

how do I preview md in vs code

Open the file, then hit the preview key.

Ctrl+Shift+V — opens the Markdown preview in the current tab. Ctrl+K then V — opens it beside the editor, so you can type on the left and watch it update on the right. This is the one you want for editing.

Three other ways to reach it, if the shortcut doesn't stick:

  • Right-click the editor tab → Open Preview (or Open Preview to the Side).
  • The magnifying-glass-with-a-page icon in the top-right corner of the editor, next to the split-editor button. It only appears when the file is recognised as Markdown.
  • Command palette (Ctrl+Shift+P) → type Markdown: Open Preview.

Scrolling

By default the preview scrolls independently. To make it follow your cursor — so the place you're editing stays in view — turn on sync:

Ctrl+Shift+P → Markdown: Toggle Preview Scroll Sync.

Or set it permanently in settings.json (Ctrl+Shift+P → Preferences: Open User Settings (JSON)):

json
{  "markdown.preview.scrollPreviewWithEditor": true,  "markdown.preview.scrollEditorWithPreview": true}

Live update

The preview refreshes as you type, no save needed. If it feels laggy on a large file, Ctrl+Shift+P → Developer: Reload Window.

Your diagrams

VS Code's preview renders Mermaid out of the box — no extension, no CDN. So the two mermaid blocks in db-README.md will draw as actual diagrams when you preview it. This is the one place you get that for free; the terminal tools we discussed (glow, bat) won't.

Two small caveats:

  • Open the folder, not just the file. If you open db-README.md as a loose file rather than opening the project folder, VS Code still previews it fine, but it can't resolve relative paths or show you the repo structure. code . from the pricejob/backend directory is the clean way in.
  • Tables render, but they don't wrap. A wide table in the preview will scroll horizontally rather than fold. Your table of tables in the README is narrow enough that this won't bite.

If you want the public-facing version on Netsite, the preview is only for your own editing — you'd still need the pandoc or mmdc route to produce an HTML file the site can serve.

Could you just explain what pushed_state and push_runs tables are showing in the db with this code:

Adding files to the workspace
Searching your files
Reading a file
Done

The script answers this quite precisely, because the docstring states the design philosophy up front: "Databasen er sandheden; webserveren er et cachet spejl af den" — the database is the truth, the webserver is a cached mirror of it. The two tables are the two halves of that mirror.

pushed_state — what is currently out there

One row per calendar day that has been uploaded, keyed on day (date, primary key).

ColumnRole
dayThe Danish calendar day this row is about
pushed_atWhen we last pushed it
rows_pushedHow many price rows that day contained
content_hashHash of the day's generated content

This is state, not history — one row per day, upserted rather than appended. record_pushed() writes it with ON CONFLICT (day) DO UPDATE, so re-pushing a day replaces the row. There is never more than one row for a given day.

The key insight is what this table means: it is not a log of "what we sent", it is a declaration of what exists at Netsite right now. That's what makes the catch-up logic work. The backlog is defined in the docstring as "dage der findes i DB men ikke står i pushed_state" — days that exist in the database but aren't in pushed_state. So the table doubles as the "already sent" filter, and if it's lost, the entire backlog replays.

content_hash is what makes re-pushing a day necessary or unnecessary. plan_window() reads the whole table into a {day: hash} dict via pushed_hashes(), and that map determines the window floor: if there's anything in it, floor = min(known). So the table also sets how far back the job bothers to look.

And --rebuild shows the escape hatch clearly: forget_pushed() does a plain DELETE FROM pushed_state WHERE day = ANY(...), wiping the rows so the next pass sees everything as unsent and uploads the lot.

push_runs — what we did each time

One row per execution of the script, keyed on run_id (bigserial). This is pure append-only logging — nothing is ever updated except the row for the run in progress.

ColumnRole
run_idIdentity of this execution
started_at / finished_atWhen it ran; finished_at is NULL while in flight
statusrunning → ok / failed / dry_run
days_plannedDays the window produced
days_uploadedDays actually transferred
days_skippedDays already current, not re-sent
bytes_uploadedTotal transferred
errorFailure reason, if any

db_start_run() inserts with status='running' and returns the run_id; db_finish_run() closes it out with finished_at = now() plus the stats. This is the same run/state shape as your sync_runs/sync_state pair — the same pattern applied to the push side rather than the collect side.

The stats come from the plan: days_planned is len(plan.daily), days_uploaded is len(plan.daily) after a successful transfer, days_skipped is the count of days whose hash already matched, and bytes_uploaded is sum(p.stat().st_size for p in plan.files()). The dry_run path closes the run with status='dry_run' and bytes_uploaded=0, so a dry run still leaves a trace without pretending to have sent anything.

The distinction in one line

pushed_state answers "what is out there right now?" — one row per day, mutating, the mirror. push_runs answers "what did we attempt, and how did it go?" — one row per attempt, immutable, the log.

That's why they're separate tables and not one. They have different cardinality (per-day vs per-execution), different mutability (upsert vs append), and different readers — the code queries pushed_state for control flow, and push_runs is for a human or a notification script looking at what happened.

Two details worth noting while you're in here

pushed_state is the single point of truth for the whole catch-up design, which makes it also the single point of failure. If it's dropped or truncated, nothing breaks — the next run just sees every day as unsent and re-uploads all of them. That's the intended recovery path, and it's graceful. But it means the table's absence is silent: you can't tell from pushed_state alone that this just happened. If that ever matters, push_runs.days_uploaded spiking is the signal.

The running rows can leak. db_start_run() inserts running before the work; if the process is killed rather than raising (OOM, kill -9, power loss), db_finish_run() never runs and the row stays running with finished_at IS NULL. The script handles the ordinary exception path carefully — the comment about rolling back first, so a failed earlier statement doesn't leave the connection in an aborted transaction and bury the real error — but it can't handle a SIGKILL. That's the same stuck-job query I put in the README's section 4.5:

sql
SELECT run_id, started_at  FROM push_runs WHERE status = 'running'   AND started_at < now() - interval '1 hour';

Given the docstring's note that the job deliberately exits 0 on Netsite downtime (so systemd doesn't report Failed every hour), a leaked running row is the only reliable way you'd notice a push job that actually died rather than one that's merely waiting for the network.

sync_runs and sync_state then

Searching your files
Searching your files
Done

Here the picture is different — and the difference is worth seeing clearly, because these two tables belong to the collect job, not the push job. This script only reads one of them.

sync_state — where the collect job has got to

This is the counterpart to pushed_state, on the other side of the pipeline. One row per job, keyed on job, updated in place:

ColumnRole
jobWhich job this row tracks — here 'dayahead_prices'
last_run_atLast time it ran, success or not
last_success_atLast time it actually worked
watermark_dkHow far forward the data reaches
rows_totalRunning total collected

The script names the job it cares about at line 138 — DB_JOB = "dayahead_prices" — and that constant exists purely so this file can look up a row that a different program writes. collect_watermark() is the only place sync_state is touched:

sql
SELECT watermark_dk FROM sync_state WHERE job = %s

That query is the whole relationship. And the docstring on that function is explicit about the scope of it: "Bruges KUN til at begrænse, hvor langt tilbage vi gider bygge ved første kørsel — ikke til at styre hvad der sendes." Used only to limit how far back we bother building on first run — not to control what gets sent.

That's a precise boundary and it's the right one. sync_state says how much raw data exists in prices. It says nothing about what Netsite has. Those are different questions with different answers, which is exactly why there are two tables.

You can see the distinction in plan_window(). The watermark is a floor, never a ceiling:

python
floor = today - timedelta(days=max_days)wm = collect_watermark(conn)if wm is not None:    wm_day = wm.astimezone(CPH).date()    floor = max(floor, wm_day - timedelta(days=1))

Two separate clamps, and the more restrictive wins — max() of two floors. Then two more clamps follow: never further back than today - max_days, and never before the first data actually present. So sync_state is one input among four, and it only ever applies on a cold start — note that it sits in the else branch, reached only when pushed_hashes() came back empty. Once pushed_state has rows, the watermark is never consulted at all.

That's a nice piece of design: the expensive question ("how much history should we rebuild?") only gets asked when you have no better information, and when you do — the mirror's own record — that takes over.

sync_runs — how the collect job went

Not touched by this file at all. No SELECT, no INSERT. Zero references in the whole script.

And that's correct, not an omission. sync_runs logs fetch attempts — what happened when we pulled data from the upstream API. This script doesn't fetch anything; it reads from Postgres and pushes to Netsite. Writing a row into sync_runs here would corrupt the meaning of the table, which is job-stamped for a reason: a reader asking "how did the dayahead_prices fetch go yesterday?" should never find push-related rows mixed in.

The four tables, side by side

Collect sidePush side
State (where are we)sync_state — watermark into pricespushed_state — what's uploaded
Log (what happened)sync_runs — fetch attemptspush_runs — push attempts
Written bycollect jobthis script

It's the same two-table pattern mirrored across the pipeline, and the mirrored naming is not accidental. sync_state/sync_runs for the sync step; pushed_state/push_runs for the push step. Same shape, same conventions, different domains — which is precisely the property that makes the weather job cheap to add later. A new source gets weather_dmi into sync_state and sync_runs and needs no new tables at all.

One observation about the coupling

The two halves are joined by exactly one string: DB_JOB = "dayahead_prices" at line 138. If the collect job ever changes the value it writes under, this lookup silently returns None — collect_watermark() returns None when the row is missing or the value is null — and the only consequence is that the floor falls back to today - max_days.

That's a genuinely benign failure: the push job just rebuilds a bit more conservatively than it might have. But it is silent, and it's the kind of string-match coupling I flagged in the README as the convention holding these tables together rather than a foreign key. Worth noting in the conventions section that sync_state.job and the DB_JOB constant must move together — because nothing in the schema will tell you if they drift apart.
